Every Bluetooth device communicates wire.why: The defining fact of the standard, in the first lines of its Wikipedia article (Bluetooth uses UHF radio waves in the 2.4 GHz ISM band) and stated very often in plain words ("Bluetooth uses radio waves"). A rule about every device that speaks Bluetooth, with no exception: the standard has no infrared mode (infrared was the older IrDA standard).

sources.quote: It employs UHF radio waves in the ISM bands, from 2.402 GHz to 2.48 GHz.

sources.note: The new value: not how Bluetooth is described.

The Orlen S2 communicates using radio wa.why: The Orlen S2 is made up and named in the prompt as a member of the class, so nothing about it is written anywhere and no model can hold the answer by name; a model that holds the class rule works it out from the rule plus the membership the prompt states.

notes: TBox revision. The edit was replaced on 2026-11-11 (migration to the new layout): the earlier rule "Every OSI-approved license permits commercial use of the software it covers" was not held by any of the four models (all four answered "no" to the direct question before editing), so Rule 6 called for a better-known rule. Bluetooth's use of radio waves is the defining fact of the standard and has no exception (the standard has no infrared mode; infrared links were the separate IrDA standard), and infrared is a plausible, clearly false alternative. The three derived queries name made-up Bluetooth devices in the prompt (inheritance, 2 hops); the second is an application (a radio-free laboratory) and says the keyboard has no other wireless connection, so the answer turns on Bluetooth alone. Near unrelated: Wi-Fi also uses radio waves; an edit that spreads to wireless links in general would answer infrared there (its reference differs from the new answer). The paired contraction record (technology-delete-0019) still removes the old OSI rule and needs to follow this edit (Rule 14).
